description: Moving from backend into ML engineering. The engineering half transfers almost entirely — what you are actually acquiring is modelling judgement and the discipline of honest evaluation. Most people underestimate the evaluation part and over-invest in model architectures.

requiredSkills.name: python
requiredSkills.note: You likely have this already; the ML ecosystem assumes fluency

requiredSkills.name: machine learning
requiredSkills.note: Framing, features, and evaluation matter more than architectures

requiredSkills.name: pytorch
requiredSkills.note: The training framework you will be expected to know

requiredSkills.name: vector search
requiredSkills.note: Increasingly assumed for retrieval and RAG work

milestones.title: Foundations — ML fundamentals and honest evaluation
Production ML — serving, monitoring, and retrieval

description: The mid-to-senior step is not about writing more code. It is about owning ambiguous problems end to end, making trade-offs you can defend in writing, and being someone other engineers' work depends on. Most people who stall here are technically ready and have not built the ownership record.

requiredSkills.name: system design
requiredSkills.note: The single biggest differentiator at this step

requiredSkills.name: postgres
requiredSkills.note: Deep knowledge of at least one datastore is expected

requiredSkills.name: kubernetes
requiredSkills.note: Seniors are expected to debug their own production

requiredSkills.name: technical leadership
requiredSkills.note: Mentoring and design review, not management

milestones.title: Depth — master the datastore and runtime you already use
Design — write and defend three real design documents
Ownership — lead one cross-team project end to end

description: The IC-to-manager move is a change of profession, not a promotion. Your output becomes your team's output, and the feedback loop lengthens from hours to quarters. The people who do this well usually trialled it as a tech lead first — and a meaningful number go back to IC, which is a normal outcome and not a failure.

requiredSkills.name: technical leadership
requiredSkills.note: Start before the title: lead projects, mentor, run reviews

requiredSkills.name: system design
requiredSkills.note: You stop building but must still hold the architecture

milestones.title: Tech lead trial — own a project's direction, not its code
People practice — mentor two engineers, run hiring loops, give hard feedback
Architecture stewardship — hold the design bar without writing the code

description: Frontend to full-stack is mostly about becoming genuinely comfortable with data and its failure modes. The language rarely blocks people; schema design, transactions, and what happens when the network is unreliable are what do.

requiredSkills.name: typescript
requiredSkills.note: You have this; it carries straight to the server

requiredSkills.name: postgres
requiredSkills.note: Schema design and transactions are the real gap

requiredSkills.name: docker
requiredSkills.note: Enough to run and debug your own stack

milestones.title: Data foundations — schema design, indexes, transactions
Ship and operate one service you wrote yourself

description: Platform engineering is product engineering where your users are other engineers. The technical skills are learnable in months; the harder shift is treating internal tooling as a product with users who can and will route around you.

requiredSkills.name: terraform
requiredSkills.note: Module design and state management, not just resource blocks

requiredSkills.name: aws
requiredSkills.note: IAM is the part that actually takes time

requiredSkills.name: kubernetes
requiredSkills.note: Expected as the substrate almost everywhere

requiredSkills.name: go
requiredSkills.note: Most platform tooling you will extend is written in it

milestones.title: Infrastructure as code, properly — modules and state
Cloud depth, with IAM as the main event
Operate the substrate — run and debug a real cluster
